worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${e}^{2x}={({e}^{x})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u={e}^{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2x}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{x})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡{e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
